packs.title: AI Engineer interview (interviewer view)
packs.blurb: LLM, systems, Python, RAG, and production trade-offs from the PropTech Founder interviewer-perspective video.

hints: They predict the next token.
Text is tokenized, then embedded.
Self-attention scores how tokens relate.
questions.rubric:
LLMs are probabilistic next-token prediction engines trained on massive web-scale data.

Text is tokenized into numeric chunks, turned into embeddings, and run through self-attention so the model can score how tokens relate. It then returns probability scores for the next token.

hints: They see the whole sequence at once, unlike RNNs.
Self-attention weights every token against every other token.
That is how they tell financial bank from river bank.
questions.rubric:
Unlike RNNs that go word-by-word, Transformers process the entire sequence at once.

Self-attention decides how much weight each token gives every other token, so the model can pick up context — financial bank vs river bank.

questions.text: How would you design a workflow that finds and replaces dead links across hundreds of client blog posts you can reach via API or HTML?
hints: Parse HTML, then HEAD the links.
Keep a window of surrounding text.
Let the LLM rewrite without the missing URL.
questions.rubric:
Parse the blog HTML with regex or BeautifulSoup.

Probe each link with HTTP HEAD — cheaper and faster than GET.

If it is dead, store the link span and a context window (about ±50 characters).

Pass that context to an LLM to rewrite the sentence so it no longer depends on the missing link.

questions.text: When would you use real-time processing versus batch processing for updates?
hints: Real-time when freshness drives the decision.
Batch when a delay is fine, like nightly embeddings.
Batch is cheaper and easier to retry.
questions.rubric:
Real-time when data freshness is critical for an immediate decision (fraud detection). It is expensive, needs always-on streams, and failure recovery is hard.

Batch when delay is acceptable — nightly knowledge-base embedding generation. Cheaper, easier to debug, simple to retry on failure.

questions.text: How would you ingest structured, unstructured, and high-volume event data in one system?
hints: SKUs go in SQL.
Reviews go to a vector index.
Logs go through Kafka or ClickHouse.
questions.rubric:
Structured data (SKUs, inventory): PostgreSQL or similar — strict schema and ACID.

Unstructured (reviews, documents): chunk, embed, index in a vector DB like Pinecone.

High-volume events/logs: buffer on Kafka, or land in ClickHouse — columnar, millions of rows/sec, high compression.

questions.text: How do you handle race conditions in asynchronous systems?
hints: A lock so only one worker mutates shared state.
Or stop sharing mutable state.
Tuples force copies instead of in-place edits.
questions.rubric:
Use a mutex — threading.Lock() — so only one worker mutates shared state at a time.

Prefer immutable structures (tuple). Functions then return copies instead of editing in place, which removes a class of races.

questions.text: What is the Global Interpreter Lock, and how do you get parallelism in Python despite it?
hints: One mutex per process.
Threads will not give you CPU parallelism.
multiprocessing gives you separate interpreters.
questions.rubric:
The GIL is a single mutex in CPython. It blocks true multi-threaded CPU-parallel execution inside one process.

Workaround: spawn processes with multiprocessing so each has its own interpreter.

questions.text: What are common async pitfalls in Python?
hints: Blocking the event loop.
time.sleep and requests instead of async I/O.
Forgetting to await a coroutine.
questions.rubric:
Blocking the event loop with CPU-heavy work or sync I/O — time.sleep() or requests instead of httpx.

Unawaited coroutines fail silently and are ugly to debug in production.
questions.answer:

questions.text: How do you handle data quality and deduplication before you embed a corpus?
hints: Exact dupes by hash.
Near-dupes with MinHash or cosine.
Normalize units and strip HTML first.
questions.rubric:
Exact duplicates: match document hashes.

Near-duplicates: MinHash / Jaccard on shingles, or cosine on embeddings, and drop pairs over a threshold (for example >90% overlap).

Normalize before tokenize: one unit system ($5 vs 5 million), strip noisy HTML.

questions.text: How do you optimize what you embed and how you query a vector index?
hints: Embed titles and descriptions, not SKUs.
Filter price and stock in SQL.
Expand short queries or use HyDE.
questions.rubric:
Embed titles and semantic descriptions. Leave price, stock, and SKUs out of the vector — those are exact/keyword filters on a normal DB.

For queries: rewrite short multi-turn prompts into a standalone question, or use HyDE — generate a hypothetical answer, embed that, and search.

questions.text: How do you handle model hallucinations in a RAG system?
hints: Drop weak retrieval hits.
Tell the model to say I do not know.
Check citations against the source.
questions.rubric:
Drop retrieved chunks below a similarity threshold.

Ground the system prompt: if it is not in the context, say "I do not know."

Post-process: citation matching so every claim maps to a source document.

questions.text: What is the AI engineering trilemma between relevancy, latency, and cost, and how do you move each side?
hints: You rarely get all three.
Cache and smaller models cut latency.
Re-rankers raise relevancy and add latency.
questions.rubric:
Relevancy, latency, and cost pull against each other. You pick two and pay on the third.

Reduce latency: semantic cache (Cloudflare AI Gateway), smaller models, fewer embedding dimensions. Relevancy can drop.

Reduce cost: trim the system prompt, route easy work to a small model. The pipeline gets more moving parts.

Maximize relevancy: cross-encoder re-rankers on the top vector hits before generation, or chain-of-thought. You pay latency and tokens.
questions.answer:
Relevancy, latency, and cost pull against each other. You pick two and pay on the third.

Reduce latency: semantic cache (Cloudflare AI Gateway), smaller models, fewer embedding dimensions. Relevancy can drop.

Reduce cost: trim the system prompt, route easy work to a small model. The pipeline gets more moving parts.

Maximize relevancy: cross-encoder re-rankers on the top vector hits before generation, or chain-of-thought. You pay latency and tokens.
